result.summary: Aeneas lands at Cumae, consults the Sibyl, buries Misenus, and plucks the golden bough. With the Sibyl he descends to the underworld, meets Palinurus, Dido and Deiphobus, and sees Tartarus and Elysium. Anchises there explains the souls' cycle and shows him the future heroes of Rome, then sends him out by the ivory gate.

scenes.title: Landing at Cumae, Apollo's temple
scenes.summary: The fleet lands at Cumae. Aeneas goes to the temple of Apollo, where Daedalus' carved doors are admired until the Sibyl calls him in and is seized by the god.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas needs the god's guidance to reach a settled home in Italy.

scenes.title: Prayer and the Sibyl's prophecy
scenes.summary: Aeneas prays; the Sibyl prophesies war in Latium and, when he asks to see his father, tells him to find the golden bough and bury his dead friend.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas risks failing to reach Latium and his father's shade.

scenes.title: Misenus buried, golden bough found
scenes.summary: The Trojans find Misenus dead, build his pyre and tomb, and Aeneas finds the golden bough, guided by doves.
scenes.stakes: Without the bough, Aeneas cannot enter the underworld.

scenes.title: Sacrifice and entering the underworld
scenes.summary: Sacrifices are offered at the cave of Avernus and the pair descend past the monstrous shapes at the threshold.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas risks death in the realm of the dead.

scenes.title: Charon and Palinurus
scenes.summary: At the Styx Aeneas meets the unburied, speaks with Palinurus, and Charon is persuaded by the golden bough to ferry them.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas cannot cross while living unless Charon accepts the bough.

scenes.title: Cerberus, judges and Dido
scenes.summary: Cerberus is drugged; Aeneas passes Minos and the Mourning Fields, where Dido refuses his plea and flees to Sychæus.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas seeks Dido's forgiveness for abandoning her.

scenes.title: Warriors and Deiphobus
scenes.summary: Aeneas meets Trojan and Greek warriors, then the mutilated Deiphobus, who tells how Helen betrayed him.
scenes.stakes: Time is running short for the descent.

scenes.title: Tartarus described
scenes.summary: Aeneas sees the walls of Tartarus; the Sibyl describes its punishments and sinners.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas is horrified by the punishments of guilt.

scenes.title: Elysium and Anchises
scenes.summary: Aeneas fixes the bough at Elysium's gate, finds Anchises, who explains purification and rebirth of souls by Lethe.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas longs to embrace his father, who slips away as a phantom.

scenes.title: Parade of Roman heroes
scenes.summary: Anchises shows his descendants from Silvius to Augustus and Marcellus, then sends Aeneas out by the ivory gate to the fleet.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas must take on the future of Rome and the coming wars in Latium.

alias_notes.explanation: Both names are used for the god of prophecy.
Patronymic of Hercules, grandson of Alcaeus.
Name for the lord of the underworld.
Name for Aeneas' people, from Teucer.

notable_quotes.reason: The famous line that descending to the underworld is easy, returning is the labour.
Anchises states Rome's mission: govern nations, spare the humbled, crush the proud.
Anchises' lament for the young Marcellus.

analysis.text: The descent links personal duty to Rome's destiny: Aeneas accepts his fate through his father's vision.
The parade of heroes culminates in Augustus and Marcellus, glorifying the Augustan regime.

legacy.text: Virgil's underworld shaped Dante's Inferno (c. 1320), where Virgil himself guides the poet.
The phrase 'the golden bough' inspired Frazer's anthropological work The Golden Bough (1890).

fun_facts.text: The Sibyl's cave at Cumae and nearby Lake Avernus are real sites that visitors can see today.

language_notes.text: "Gives rope to his fleet" means he lets out the ships' cables, setting sail freely; "wafted" means carried gently.
The anchor's "griping fang" is its curved, gripping prong; the ships are moored stern-first with anchors and their curved hulls line the shore.
Hesperian means western, the Greek name for Italy; "seed of fire" is sparks struck from flint.
The Trivian goddess is Diana (Hecate), "of the three ways"; her grove stands beside Apollo's temple.
Dædalus fled King Minos of Crete on wings he made, after building the Labyrinth; Phœbus is Apollo.
Androgeos, son of Minos, was killed in Athens; in revenge Minos made Athens (sons of Cecrops) send seven youths yearly to the Minotaur.
Pasiphaë, Minos' wife, was cursed with desire for a bull; the Minotaur was her child.
The royal princess is Ariadne, who loved Theseus; Dædalus told her to give him a thread to escape the maze.
Icarus, Dædalus' son, flew too near the sun and fell into the sea; his father could not depict him.
"Bespeaks" means addresses; the Sibyl here is named Deïphobe, priestess of Apollo and Diana.
Phœbus (Apollo) guided the arrow that killed Achilles, here called Æacides as grandson of Æacus. Paris shot it.
Massylian: of the Massyli, a North African people near Carthage, which Æneas has just left.
Pergamus is the citadel of Troy, used for Troy itself.
Trivian sister: Diana, called Trivia as goddess of crossroads and linked with Hecate.
The Sibyl wrote prophecies on leaves, which the wind could scatter; Æneas asks her to speak them aloud.
Another Achilles is Turnus, the Italian champion. The alien bride is Lavinia, whose marriage causes war, as Helen's did.
The Grecian town is Pallanteum, where the Arcadian Greek king Evander will become Æneas's ally.
Orpheus, Pollux, Theseus and Alcides (Hercules) all entered the underworld and returned; Æneas claims descent from Jove like them.
The Juno of the shades is Proserpine, queen of the underworld; the golden bough is her offering.
Clarion is a shrill war trumpet; Misenus is a trumpeter whose music rouses soldiers to battle.
Triton is a sea-god, son of Neptune, who blew a conch shell; Misenus's challenge to him is a pride that offends the gods.
"Carry it into the sky" is hyperbole for building the pyre very high.
The golden branch is the offering the Sibyl said must be carried to Proserpine to enter the underworld.
Doves were sacred to Venus, Æneas's mother, so he recognizes them as her messengers.
Avernus is a lake near Cumae believed to be an entrance to the underworld; "noisome" means foul-smelling.
Foil means thin metal leaf; it describes the golden leaves tinkling in the breeze.
Teucrians is another name for the Trojans, from their ancestor Teucer.
Averted eyes follow the ancestral custom of lighting the pyre while looking away.
Sprinkling water with an olive branch is a ritual purification of mourners after contact with death.
Aornos is Greek for 'birdless'; the name was given to Avernus, the lake and cave near Cumae, because birds were said to die in its fumes.
Chargers are large shallow dishes; here they are bowls used to catch the sacrificial blood.
The Furies' mother is Night, and her 'mighty sister' is Earth; the lamb is black, suiting powers of darkness.
Phlegethon is the underworld river of fire; Chaos here is the primeval void, invoked as a power of the shades.
'Niggard' means stingy; the moon gives only a grudging, scanty light.
Fillets are ribbons or headbands, here bloody and bound in the Fury Strife's snake hair.
The 'portent of Lerna' is the Hydra, a many-headed serpent later killed by Hercules.
Tartarean: of Tartarus, the deepest part of the underworld. Acheron and Cocytus are underworld rivers.
Styx was the river by which gods swore their most binding oaths; breaking such an oath brought severe punishment.
Apollo had given Aeneas an oracle promising he would reach Italy; Ausonian means Italian.
Phœbus' tripod: the seat of Apollo's priestess at Delphi, used here for his oracles.
Ween means 'think' or 'suppose'; adjure means 'solemnly beg'.
Alcides is Hercules, who dragged Cerberus from the underworld; Theseus and Pirithous tried to carry off Proserpine.
Amphrysian refers to the Sibyl, a priestess of Apollo, who once served at Amphrysus in legend.
The Sibyl switches to 'thou', a more formal, solemn address, as she confronts Charon.
The "morsel steeped in the slumber of honey" is a drugged honey-cake; "medicated meal" means grain mixed with sleep-inducing herbs.
"The river without return" is the Acheron, which the dead cannot recross; Æneas is the exception, as a living visitor.
"Portionless of the sweets of life" means cheated of life's pleasures; "black death-day" is the day of their death.
"Urn in hand": Minos shakes the urn of lots to select the jurors and cases; "cognizance" means judicial examination.
These are women and figures from myth who died through love; Cæneus was born a woman, changed to a man by Neptune, and here returns to female form.
Marpessa was a mountain on the island of Paros, famed for its hard white marble.
Sychæus was Dido's first husband, murdered by her brother Pygmalion; in the underworld she is reunited with him.
Dardan means Trojan, after Dardanus, legendary ancestor of the Trojan royal house.
'Would fain' means would gladly; the ghosts eagerly want to linger and walk beside him.
Danaans is a common Homeric name for the Greeks; 'erst' means formerly.
An empty tomb (cenotaph) with a thrice-repeated call to the spirit honoured the dead whose bodies were not recovered, so the shade could rest.
The 'Spartan woman' is Helen, who after Paris's death became Deiphobus's wife, then betrayed him to Menelaus.
The 'child of Æolus' is Ulysses, here slandered with a claim of Æolus as his father in some traditions.
Dis is the king of the underworld; Elysium is the abode of the blessed, Tartarus the place of punishment.
Phlegethon is the underworld river of fire; "Tartarean" means belonging to Tartarus, the deep prison of the damned.
Adamant is a legendary unbreakable substance, here used for the gate's pillars.
Teucrians are the Trojans, named after their ancestor Teucer.
"Gnosian" means of Gnossus (Cnossos) in Crete, where Rhadamanthus had been a king.
The sons of Aloeus, Otus and Ephialtes, tried to storm heaven by piling mountains on one another.
Salmoneus, king of Elis, imitated Jove's thunder and lightning and demanded worship as a god.
Tityos, a giant, assaulted Latona and was punished with a vulture eternally eating his regrowing liver.
The rolling stone is Sisyphus's punishment, and the wheel is Ixion's; Theseus is here said to sit eternally.
The Cyclopes were the divine smiths; the walls and gates here are those of Pluto's palace, where Aeneas must leave the golden bough.
"Pleasaunces" is an archaic word for pleasure grounds or gardens.
"Ether" is the pure, bright upper air breathed by gods; "plenitude" means fullness.
The Thracian priest is Orpheus, the legendary singer who played the lyre; the seven notes refer to its seven strings.
Teucer was an early king of Troy's land; Ilus, Assaracus and Dardanus are ancestors of the Trojan royal line.
A "pæan" is a joyful song of praise, often addressed to Apollo.
A "fillet" is a headband; "cinctured" means encircled.
Musæus was a legendary early Greek poet, here honoured as chief of the blessed bards.
The thrice-failed embrace echoes the scene in Homer's Odyssey where Ulysses cannot hold his mother's shade.
"Titan" here means the Sun; the passage expresses a Stoic and Platonic idea of a world-soul.
"The pointless spear" is a headless spear, a sign of a young man not yet fought in war; "fill the next place in light" means he will be next to be born.
"Civic oak" is the oak-leaf crown given to a Roman who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle.
"Child of a god": Augustus was the adopted son of Julius Caesar, who was deified. Saturn's reign in Latium was the legendary golden age.
Alcides is Hercules. The brazen-footed deer, the Erymanthian boar and the Lernaean hydra were among his labours; Bacchus' travels to India are also invoked.
Brutus the avenger expelled the Tarquin kings and became one of Rome's first consuls. The fasces were bundles of rods and axes carried before magistrates as symbols of authority.
The father-in-law and son-in-law are Julius Caesar, who crossed the Alps, and Pompey, who led eastern forces, in the civil war.
This refers to Fabius Maximus, who saved Rome from Hannibal by delaying tactics; the line echoes Ennius.
Marcellus, Augustus' nephew and heir, died young in 23 BC. Lilies were strewn on graves as a funeral offering.
The two gates of Sleep: true dreams pass through horn, false ones through ivory. Aeneas leaves by ivory, a famously puzzling choice.

context_notes.text: Cumæ, on the Italian coast near Naples, was an early Greek colony from Eubœa, hence "Eubœan".
The Sibyl was a prophetess at Cumæ; Apollo, who also had an oracle at Delos, inspired her.
The cave with a hundred openings is the Sibyl's oracle, from which her answers echo out.
The Teucrians are the Trojans, named after their early king Teucer.
The Sibyl of Cumæ is a priestess possessed by Apollo when prophesying; her resistance shows the god's violent control.
The unburied friend is Misenus, the trumpeter; unburied dead were thought to pollute the living.
Hector was the chief Trojan warrior, killed by Achilles in the Trojan War.
Cypress was associated with death and mourning, which is why it is placed before the pyre.
The headland near Naples, Cape Misenum, is traditionally named for Misenus.
Hecate was a goddess of night, magic and the crossroads, linked with both heaven and the underworld (Erebus).
Proserpine is queen of the underworld, wife of the Stygian monarch (Pluto), who is honoured in the next sentence.
The priestess is the Sibyl of Cumae, who guides Æneas through the underworld.
The elm of false dreams stands at the gate; Roman tradition imagined dreams as lingering in such a place.
Charon is the underworld ferryman who carries the dead across the river.
Roman belief held that the unburied could not rest until given proper funeral rites.
The guardian is Cerberus, the three-headed dog of the underworld; Proserpine is Pluto's wife and, here, niece.
The golden bough was the Sibyl's required offering to Proserpine, granting a living man entry to the underworld.
Cerberus is the three-headed hound guarding the entrance to the underworld, keeping the dead in and the living out.
Minos, legendary king of Crete, serves as a judge of the dead in the underworld.
Styx is the underworld river by which gods swore oaths; here it winds nine times around the unburied suicides.
Dido, queen of Carthage, killed herself after Æneas left her, as told in Book 4.
Tydeus, Parthenopæus and Adrastus were heroes of the legendary expedition of the Seven against Thebes.
Deiphobus, a son of Priam, was mutilated by the Greeks when Troy fell; the ghost keeps the wounds of his death.
The Sibyl is the priestess of Apollo guiding Æneas through the underworld.
Tisiphone is one of the three Furies, goddesses of vengeance who punish crime in the underworld.
The priestess is the Sibyl of Cumae, guide to Aeneas; Hecate, goddess of witchcraft and the underworld, put her in charge of Avernus's groves.
Rhadamanthus was a legendary Cretan lawgiver who became a judge of the dead.
The Hydra was a many-headed monster; here it guards the inner pit of Tartarus.
The Titans were older gods who fought Jove and were cast into Tartarus.
The Tyrrhene deep is the Tyrrhenian sea off Italy, where Æneas' fleet waits at Cumae.
Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in the underworld; souls drink it before returning to life.
Virgil describes purgatorial cleansing by wind, water and fire, with Elysium as the final home of the few fully purified.
Anchises, Aeneas' dead father, shows him the future Roman heroes waiting as souls in the underworld before birth.
Romulus, son of Mars, is Rome's legendary founder; his grandsire is Numitor, king of Alba Longa.
Iulus was Aeneas' son; the Julian family, including Julius Caesar and Augustus, claimed descent from him.
Mummius conquered Corinth, and another Roman will conquer Greece (Argos, Mycenæ), avenging Troy against the Greeks.
Marcellus defeated Gauls in 222 BC and won the spolia opima, the highest military honour, for the third time in Roman history.

literary_notes.text: The narrator's cry "O cruel woe!" breaks in with personal emotion over the sacrificed youths.
"Inextricable" is repeated to stress the maze's complexity before Dædalus' pity resolves it.
"Twice... twice" shows a father's grief overcoming his art, a moving image of failure.
Rapid physical changes, from her hue and hair to her growing size, show the god's possession; the tense shift adds immediacy.
Apollo's control of the Sibyl is imagined as a horse tamed with a bit and goad.
The vision of the Tiber foaming with blood previews the war with the Latins in the later books.
Robing truth in darkness captures the riddling nature of oracles.
The easy descent is set against the hard return, stressing the labour of the journey.
The endlessly renewed golden bough suggests the underworld's lasting power and the need for fate's permission.
The Trojans' question about who is dead is answered suddenly; the repeated name emphasizes the shock of the discovery.
Misenus's challenge to the gods and his sudden death show the classic pattern of pride punished.
"Æneas the good" is a recurring epithet stressing his piety and compassion as a leader.
The doves appear just after Æneas prays, showing divine favor and guiding the plot.
The gold among dark oak is compared to mistletoe growing on a tree in winter, suggesting a strange, parasitic and magical growth.
The narrator turns to address the gods of the dead directly, asking permission to describe forbidden things.
The dim passage through the underworld is compared to a walk through a wood under a clouded moon, conveying murk and uncertainty.
Abstractions such as Age, Terror, Hunger and War are given dwellings, making human woes into monsters guarding the gate.
Æneas's bold reaction would be pointless: his sword cannot harm bodiless shades, showing courage meeting something it cannot fight.
Charon's vigorous old age shows his divine nature and makes him both menacing and strange.
The crowd of dead is likened to falling autumn leaves and migrating birds, conveying their vast number and helpless drift.
Aeneas bitterly says Apollo kept his word, because the promise seemed broken by Palinurus' apparent death.
The wave is called Palinurus' home, vividly expressing his homeless, restless state.
Palinurus' joy at the land bearing his name points to the later commemoration of his memory in Italy.
The whole realm ringing with Cerberus' barking exaggerates his size and menace.
Love is imagined as a beast whose tooth eats the heart, conveying lasting, painful passion.
Dido's dim figure is likened to the new moon glimpsed through clouds, suggesting uncertainty and fading hope.
Æneas swears by sacred powers that he left unwillingly, yet his duty caused her death, which is the tragic irony of the reunion.
Dido's stony unresponsiveness is compared to flint or crag, showing her complete rejection of Æneas.
The throats 'mock' the cry, making the ghosts' failing voices seem to betray them, a vivid image of helpless fear.
Sleep is likened to the calm of death, foreshadowing his murder and underscoring his helplessness.
Helen calls herself a helpmate yet disarms her husband; she hopes the betrayal will erase her past crime.
The brief, abrupt close shows the ghost vanishing mid-speech, ending the encounter quickly and unceremoniously.
Fire, thunder and triple walls build a vivid, terrifying picture of Tartarus before any sinner appears.
Measuring the abyss as twice the distance from earth to heaven conveys its unimaginable depth.
The Sibyl cries out "Madman!" at Salmoneus, expressing her scorn and moral judgment of his arrogance.
The sinners sit before a rich feast they can never touch, so luxury itself becomes their torment.
The Sibyl refuses to describe the doom, letting its horror be imagined and heightening suspense.
The hundred tongues and iron lungs stress that the crimes and punishments are beyond human telling.
Continuity between earthly and afterlife pursuits shows the dead keeping their loves, a recurring idea in this underworld.
Anchises' rapid, emotional questions show a father's tenderness and long-held hope.
The phantom is compared to wind and to the wings of sleep, stressing its insubstantiality and Æneas' grief.
Souls are likened to humming bees on flowers, giving a gentle, busy image of countless spirits.
The body is portrayed as a blind dungeon imprisoning the soul.
A list of future kings of Alba gives Aeneas, and the reader, a preview of Rome's long destiny.
The contrast between future famous names and present nameless lands underlines how Rome's greatness will grow from obscurity.
Rome is compared to Cybele, the tower-crowned mother of gods, proud of her many divine offspring.
The emphatic repetition "This, this is he" builds a climax, as the poem's prophecy reaches Augustus, its Roman patron.
Anchises directly addresses the future Romans, pleading against civil war; the emotional appeal makes the warning urgent.
The "shadow of gloomy night" around the youth's head foreshadows his early death.
Anchises speaks directly to the young Marcellus, deepening the pathos of his lost promise.
